KEY MESSAGE 1...A nor'easter well off the coast will bring 
coastal impacts and hazardous marine conditions through 
Thursday.

A closed low off the Mid-Atlantic coast will gradually shift 
north and eastward through later this week. This will continue 
to support surface low pressure, which is forecast to strengthen
as it slowly moves north and northeastward (even meanders some 
for a time). Meanwhile, strong surface high pressure will be 
centered across northern New England today. These systems will 
result in a tightening pressure gradient into our area through 
this evening. 

While this nor'easter remains hundreds of miles off of our 
coast (an ocean storm), some impacts are still being felt for 
our coastal and marine areas. The continued north to north-
northeast wind has built the offshore seas and these will be 
breaking into the beaches resulting in beach erosion in some 
areas especially during times of high tide. The pressure 
gradient should tend to tighten some more today as the storm is
forecast to shift westward some or even make a small offshore 
loop today. This should result in the winds peaking today. For 
areas along the coast, peak wind gusts in the 30-40 mph range 
are forecast and then up to 30 mph inland. No impacts are 
expected inland given how far offshore this storm is. Some 
showers may try and approach the immediate coast though during 
the day, but overall the drier air on the west side of this 
system along with the offshore distance should keep these areas 
mainly dry. Some cloudiness should spread westward for a time 
later today into tonight, however this may be mainly the mid to
high level variety.

For Thursday and Friday, the storm will gradually head farther 
out to sea as an incoming system from the northwest kicks it 
out. This will quickly lessen the marine and coastal impacts, 
while keeping our weather dry and providing a fresh shot of 
chilly air.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A prolonged period of onshore flow will lead to
multiple elevated high tide cycles this week resulting in 
rounds of coastal flooding, with the peak being this evening.

As the nor'easter meanders offshore through the middle of the 
week, there is a persistent and strong north-northeast wind in 
place. This prolonged period of onshore flow will result in 
multiple elevated high tide cycles. Recent forecast trends have 
been lowering on the crests of the high tide cycles for this 
event.

Water levels look to peak this evening, with fairly widespread
but minor flooding from Ocean County NJ southward through
Delaware including the Delaware shores of Delaware Bay. In some
of the back bays, moderate coastal flooding is possible with 
this evening's high tide cycle. Given lowering forecasts, did 
not have the confidence to issue a Coastal Flood Watch or
Warning. One area where conditions look notably improved is
Cumberland County NJ, where the north-northeast wind should push
water away from the bay shore and thus have cancelled the
Coastal Flood Advisory there. Beyond this evening, the 
nor'easter will gradually be moving away from the region for the
end of the week. Another round of coastal flooding is possible 
Thursday evening with spotty minor to widespread minor coastal 
flooding. This high tide cycle is forecast to be lower than 
this evening's high tide cycle.

At this time we are not forecasting any coastal flooding for the 
Maryland eastern shore. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Frost impacts possible Friday night and 
Saturday night where the growing season continues. 

As an upper-level trough pivots across the Northeast on Friday,
a potentially strong mid level ridge in the Plains to Midwest 
shifts eastward some into the weekend. This will support strong 
surface high pressure initially centered near the Great Lakes, 
which then shifts eastward into the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic 
Friday and over the weekend.

A chilly and dry air mass will accompany this strong surface 
high, and as the high itself settles more overhead the winds 
will decouple. This will set the stage for efficient radiational
cooling both Friday night and Saturday night. The forecast 
lows, as of now, are in the 30s for much of the area (away from 
the coasts and outside of the urban centers) with a frost 
potential. It is possible that if the radiational cooling ends 
up being stronger, then some areas could get to freezing or a 
little below. Overall though, frost impacts are possible where 
the growing season remains active.
